title: The Owl Nebula, M97
caption: The Owl Nebula, imaged by the Burrell Schmidt telescope at Kitt Peak
celestial: M97, NGC 3587, Owl Nebula · constellation Ursa Major
credit: Karen Kwitter (Williams College), Ron Downes (STScI), You-Hua Chu (University of Illinois), and NOIRLab/NSF/AURA

recognition.text: Official NSF NOIRLab / Gemini press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: The Owl Nebula, also known as Messier 97, floats in this view as a soft, round glow, made from three sets of narrowband images taken with the Burrell Schmidt telescope at Kitt Peak National Observatory in June 1991.

The Owl is a planetary nebula: the shell of gas puffed off by a Sun-like star near the end of its life. Despite the name, planetary nebulae have nothing to do with planets; early astronomers with small telescopes thought their round disks looked like planets, and the label stuck.

Its nickname comes from two darker patches in the shell that, to many observers, look like a pair of owl's eyes staring back. Each color in the picture is the light of one element: oxygen in blue, nitrogen in green and hydrogen in red, so the image doubles as a map of the gas the star left behind.

understand.summary: Three narrowband filters on the Burrell Schmidt telescope: hydrogen-alpha shown in red, ionized nitrogen in green and doubly ionized oxygen in blue.
understand.eye: Through a telescope the Owl is a faint gray disk; the colors come from separating the light of individual elements.
